headline: A Google medical chatbot questioned 98 real patients before urgent primary-care visits in Boston, and the doctors watching never had to stop a chat for safety reasons.
score_reason: Pool 7 lowered by 1: the study came out on 8 Oct 2026, three days before the window, so this is late coverage; the headline's claim matches the article.
importance_line: It is among the first real-world safety tests of a patient-facing diagnostic chatbot, which matters to patients who already ask chatbots about symptoms and to clinics facing long waits, but it was a small, single-clinic study funded by Google's parent with no comparison group, so any benefit to care is unproven.
summary: Medical Daily reports that AMIE, Google's research chatbot that interviews patients about their symptoms and suggests possible diagnoses, questioned 98 patients before urgent primary-care visits at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston while physicians watched each chat live, and none met the study's pre-set stop rules, according to a study published in The Lancet on 8 Oct 2026. The team reported one made-up statement and one chat rated somewhat harmful; this was a small Alphabet-funded safety test with no comparison group that left out emergencies and mental health care, and AMIE is not approved for clinical use.
notes: Read in full via Medical Daily (fulltext). Study published 8 Oct 2026; earlier coverage by Google, the New York Times and others on 8-9 Oct 2026 per Google News listing.
